```{r vignette-options, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R", local = TRUE)
RUN_BAYESIAN <- identical(
  Sys.getenv("MOSTR_RUN_BAYESIAN_VIGNETTE"),
  "true"
) && requireNamespace("rstan", quietly = TRUE)
```

In longitudinal ordinal data, some visits often have no recorded state: a
questionnaire was not returned, or a patient was known to be alive but their
level of care on that day was not documented. A transition model predicts each
state from the previous one, so a single missing state affects two
transitions: the move *into* the missing visit and the move *out of* it.

`orm_markov()` fits the model on rows where both the state and the previous
state are observed. Every transition that touches a missing visit is dropped.
We call this *complete-row analysis*. `orm_markov_ml()` fits the same model
but keeps those visits: for a gap, it adds up the probabilities of every path
the patient could have taken through the missing visits. It can also use
partial information, such as "alive, level unknown".

This article shows

1. how to prepare data with missing states;
2. how to fit `orm_markov_ml()` and choose `missing_states`;
3. how to code partially known states with `rms::Ocens()`;
4. when complete-row analysis is biased and `orm_markov_ml()` is not;
5. that the fit works with `avg_sops()`, `avg_comparisons()`, and
   `inferences()`;
6. how to fit the same model with Bayesian methods, using
   `blrm_markov_ml()`.

## Example data

We simulate 400 patients for 28 days with `sim_actt2_markov()`, which mimics
the eight-state NIAID scale of the ACTT-2 trial (state 8 is death). The full
data serve as a reference: we know every state.

```{r setup}
library(mostr)
library(rms)

N_PATIENTS <- 400
FOLLOW_UP <- 28
ABSORB <- "8"

full_raw <- sim_actt2_markov(
  n_patients = N_PATIENTS,
  follow_up_time = FOLLOW_UP,
  treatment_effect = log(0.8),
  seed = 2026
)
full <- prepare_markov_data(full_raw, absorbing_state = 8)
full <- full[order(full$id, full$time), ]
```

We then delete states in a way that is common in practice: **deaths are always
recorded**, but for patients who are alive, 25% of daily states are missing
completely at random. After a missing state, the next row's previous state
`yprev` is unknown too, so we set it to `NA`.

```{r make-missing}
set.seed(1)
observed <- full
alive <- observed$y != ABSORB
drop <- alive & runif(nrow(observed)) < 0.25
observed$y[drop] <- NA
same_patient <- c(FALSE, observed$id[-1] == observed$id[-nrow(observed)])
observed$yprev[c(FALSE, drop[-nrow(observed)]) & same_patient] <- NA
mean(is.na(observed$y))
```

Keep the rows with missing states. `prepare_markov_data()` keeps them, and
`orm_markov_ml()` needs one row for every scheduled visit until death or the
end of follow-up. A visit without a row is treated as a visit that was not
scheduled, not as a missing state.

## Complete-row analysis

`orm_markov()` drops every row with a missing `y` or `yprev`:

```{r fit-cra}
formula <- y ~ rcs(time, 4) + tx + yprev
dd <- datadist(observed)
options(datadist = "dd")

fit_cra <- orm_markov(formula, data = observed, id_var = "id")
fit_full <- orm_markov(formula, data = full, id_var = "id")
c(full_rows = nrow(full), complete_rows = fit_cra$stats[["Obs"]])
```

Here this is not just less efficient: it is **biased**. Deaths are never
missing, but transitions between living states often are. Among the rows that
remain, deaths are over-represented, so complete-row analysis overstates
mortality.

## Maximum likelihood with missing states

`orm_markov_ml()` needs the patient ID (each patient's rows form one chain)
and the absorbing state(s). `missing_states` says what a missing state can
be:

* `"any"`: nothing is known about the visit; the patient may have died. Use
  this when vital status was not recorded at visits with a missing state.
* `"non_absorbing"`: the patient was alive. Use this when vital status is
  known at every visit, so a missing state never hides a death.

In our data deaths are always recorded, so `"non_absorbing"` is right. We also
fit `"any"` to see what happens when this knowledge is ignored.

```{r fit-ml}
fit_ml <- orm_markov_ml(
  formula,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorbing_state = 8,
  missing_states = "non_absorbing"
)
fit_ml_any <- orm_markov_ml(
  formula,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorbing_state = 8,
  missing_states = "any"
)
fit_ml$ml[c("loglik", "iterations", "converged", "max_abs_score",
  "missing_info_fraction", "n_missing", "n_gaps", "n_trailing")]
```

The fit converged (`converged`, and `max_abs_score` close to zero means the
log-likelihood is at its maximum). `missing_info_fraction` is the largest
share of information lost because states are missing: 0 would mean nothing is
lost, 1 that a coefficient is not informed by the data at all.

## Coding partially known states with `Ocens()`

Instead of `NA` plus a rule for all missing rows, each row can say which
states are possible. `rms::Ocens(lower, upper)` takes the lowest and highest
possible state: `Ocens(b, b)` is an observed state `b`, and `Ocens(1, 7)` is
"alive, level unknown" on this scale. Rows with observed, partially known,
and missing states can be mixed. With `Ocens(1, 7)` for every missing state,
the fit equals `missing_states = "non_absorbing"`:

```{r fit-ocens}
observed$y_lo <- ifelse(is.na(observed$y), 1, as.numeric(as.character(observed$y)))
observed$y_hi <- ifelse(is.na(observed$y), 7, as.numeric(as.character(observed$y)))

fit_ocens <- orm_markov_ml(
  Ocens(y_lo, y_hi) ~ rcs(time, 4) + tx + yprev,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorbing_state = 8
)
all.equal(coef(fit_ocens), coef(fit_ml), tolerance = 1e-8)
```

`Ocens()` is more flexible than `missing_states` because the range can differ
by row: "in hospital, level unknown" is `Ocens(3, 7)`, and "at least on
oxygen" is `Ocens(5, Inf)` (states above 4; an endpoint of `Inf` or `-Inf`
excludes the finite endpoint). Whether a state is reported exactly must not
depend on the unreported exact state.

## Comparing the fits

The table shows the threshold for death (`y>=8`, which sets the daily
mortality) and the treatment coefficient, with robust standard errors. The
full-data fit is the reference.

```{r compare-coefficients}
fits <- list(
  full_data = fit_full,
  complete_rows = fit_cra,
  ml_any = fit_ml_any,
  ml_non_absorbing = fit_ml
)
terms <- c("y>=8", "tx")
round(t(sapply(fits, function(f) {
  c(coef(f)[terms], se = sqrt(diag(vcov(f, intercepts = "all")))[terms])
})), 3)
```

Complete-row analysis moves the death threshold upwards (more deaths) and
changes the treatment coefficient. Both maximum likelihood fits agree with the
full-data fit. They are nearly identical to each other: in a gap that ends
with an observed living state, the patient cannot have died during the gap,
because death is never left. The two rules differ only for missing states at
the end of a patient's rows, where `"any"` allows a death that was not
recorded. When deaths are always recorded, `"non_absorbing"` uses that
knowledge.

## State occupancy probabilities

The fit works with the same functions as an `orm_markov()` fit. Averaged
SOPs use every patient's starting state, including patients whose later
states are mostly missing.

```{r avg-sops}
avg_ml <- avg_sops(
  fit_ml,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:FOLLOW_UP,
  absorb = ABSORB
) |>
  inferences(method = "delta", vcov = "unconditional")

avg_cra <- avg_sops(
  fit_cra,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:FOLLOW_UP,
  absorb = ABSORB
)
avg_full <- avg_sops(
  fit_full,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:FOLLOW_UP,
  absorb = ABSORB
)

death_day28 <- function(x) {
  x$estimate[x$state == ABSORB & x$time == FOLLOW_UP]
}
rbind(
  full_data = death_day28(avg_full),
  complete_rows = death_day28(avg_cra),
  ml_non_absorbing = death_day28(avg_ml)
)
```

The columns are the two arms (`tx = 0`, `tx = 1`): the probability of having
died by day 28. Complete-row analysis overstates it; the maximum likelihood
fit is close to the full-data fit.

```{r plot-sops}
plot_sops(avg_ml)
```

Treatment contrasts and their confidence intervals work the same way. As
everywhere in mostr, `times` lists consecutive visits, so we predict every day
and then show days 7, 14, and 28:

```{r comparisons}
cmp <- avg_comparisons(
  fit_ml,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:FOLLOW_UP,
  state_sets = list(death = ABSORB),
  absorb = ABSORB
) |>
  inferences(method = "delta", vcov = "unconditional")
cmp[cmp$time %in% c(7, 14, 28),
  c("time", "state_set", "estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

`inferences()` also supports `method = "mvn"`, `"score_bootstrap"`, and
`"bootstrap"` (which refits `orm_markov_ml()` on resampled patients, missing
rows included). Fractional weighted bootstrap (`"fwb"`) is not available
because `orm_markov_ml()` does not accept row weights.

## Bayesian fits

`blrm_markov_ml()` fits the Bayesian model of `blrm_markov()` with the same
handling of missing states. It uses the same likelihood as `orm_markov_ml()`
and the priors of `rmsb::blrm()`: a weak Dirichlet prior for the intercepts
and flat priors for the other coefficients, unless `pcontrast` sets a prior
for a contrast such as the treatment effect. It also accepts `ppo` and `cppo`
for constrained partial proportional odds, as `blrm_markov()` does, and
`cluster(id)` in the formula for a random intercept per patient. With random
intercepts, `avg_sops()` and `avg_comparisons()` use each patient's own
intercept when called with `include_re = TRUE`.

`blrm_markov_ml()` runs its own Stan program, which is compiled the first time
the function is used. Compiling needs a C++ toolchain (Rtools on Windows) and
takes a few minutes; the compiled program is saved and reused in later
sessions. The code in this section runs only when the environment variable
`MOSTR_RUN_BAYESIAN_VIGNETTE` is `"true"`. It uses few iterations to keep
running time short; a real analysis needs more and a check of the sampling
diagnostics.

```{r fit-bayes, eval = RUN_BAYESIAN}
fit_bayes <- blrm_markov_ml(
  formula,
  data = observed,
  id_var = "id",
  absorbing_state = 8,
  missing_states = "non_absorbing",
  iter = 1000,
  chains = 2,
  cores = 2,
  seed = 1
)
fit_bayes$diagnostics[terms, ]
```

`Rhat` close to 1 means the chains agree; `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail` are the
effective numbers of independent draws for the centre and the tails of the
posterior. With these weak priors, the posterior means and standard
deviations are close to the maximum likelihood estimates and their
model-based standard errors:

```{r compare-bayes, eval = RUN_BAYESIAN}
round(rbind(
  ml_estimate = coef(fit_ml)[terms],
  ml_se = sqrt(diag(fit_ml$ml$var_model))[terms],
  posterior_mean = coef(fit_bayes)[terms],
  posterior_sd = apply(fit_bayes$draws[, terms], 2, sd)
), 3)
```

SOP functions compute their results for each posterior draw and report the
posterior median with a 95% credible interval:

```{r avg-sops-bayes, eval = RUN_BAYESIAN}
avg_bayes <- avg_sops(
  fit_bayes,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  times = 1:FOLLOW_UP,
  absorb = ABSORB,
  n_draws = 200,
  seed = 1
)
avg_bayes[avg_bayes$state == ABSORB & avg_bayes$time == FOLLOW_UP,
  c("tx", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

## When is complete-row analysis biased?

Both methods assume that the model is right. They differ in what they assume
about why states are missing:

* **Missing depends only on the past** (for example on earlier states or
  treatment): complete-row analysis is unbiased, because which rows are kept
  says nothing about the next transition once the previous state is known.
  `orm_markov_ml()` is unbiased too and uses the rows complete-row analysis
  drops, so its standard errors are usually smaller.
* **Missing depends on later observed states**, for example when a visit is
  less often documented if the patient was discharged soon afterwards:
  complete-row analysis is biased, `orm_markov_ml()` is not (this is still
  "missing at random").
* **Missing never hides a death** (as above): complete-row analysis is
  biased, because the transitions it drops are all between living states
  (`vignette("missing-qol-recorded-deaths")` works through why).
  `"non_absorbing"` or `Ocens(1, K - 1)` is unbiased. `"any"` ignores that a
  missing state at the end of a patient's rows means "alive", which can bias
  it slightly when many patients end with missing states.
* **Missing depends on the unobserved state itself** (for example sicker
  patients skip visits more often than others in the same previous state):
  both methods are biased. This is "missing not at random"; sensitivity
  analyses are outside the scope of `orm_markov_ml()` and
  `blrm_markov_ml()`.

## Requirements and limits

* The model must be first order: transitions depend on the past only through
  `yprev` (`p_var`). Other covariates must be fixed per patient or functions
  of time. A covariate computed from the state history, such as a lagged
  state, would be wrong after a missing state. `p2_var` is not supported.
* Keep a row for every scheduled visit until an *observed* death or the end of
  follow-up. If a death may go unrecorded, the visits after it still belong
  in the data, with the death or a missing state. Ending a patient's rows at a
  missing state hides that death and, with `missing_states = "any"`, makes
  mortality look lower than it is. Applying `prepare_markov_data()` to the
  observed data keeps these rows, because it only drops rows whose `yprev` is
  an observed death.
* The starting state (`yprev` on each patient's first row) and all covariates
  must be observed. After a missing state, `yprev` is ignored; the chain is
  rebuilt from the response.
* Every state must occur as an outcome, and every non-absorbing state as a
  previous state, among transitions with both states observed, because these
  give the starting values.
